sources.headline: Thousands march to Indian Supreme Court to demand election chief resign
sources.text: Thousands of opposition supporters marched through Delhi to India's Supreme Court to demand the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud.Monday's "March for Democracy" was the latest in a series of demonstrations, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital. Thousands of protesters were detained over the weekend.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi submitted a petition to the court challenging the process, in which tens of millions of names have been struck off the voter rolls.Opposition parties allege the revision benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the BJP reject the charge.For weeks requests to protest had been denied by police, citing law and order reasons. Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained in Delhi.Gandhi called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march. In a press conference, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Chief Justice Surya Kant, laying out their concerns with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's alleged conduct.After they filed their petition later in the day, Kant responded by saying the matter was already before the court and therefore sub judice - meaning he could not speak about it.But he added: "You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law."There was a heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march, with restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some metro stations.A bus carrying Gandhi and other opposition leaders made its way to the court from Barakamba road. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind him was Neha Bora, a student leader who has gained prominence in the protests.A few kilometres on, in a place called Mandi House, the bus stopped and Rahul Gandhi and a few others climbed on top of the vehicle to wave at supporters lining up the street in the thousands. Many protesters climbed on to other buses parked here, while some waved flags and chanted anti-government slogans to the sound of drums and lots of cheering."If they take away our right to vote, what is left with us?" one protester asked an AFP news agency reporter. Another protester called the march "a fight to save the very fabric" of India, the world's largest democracy.Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.The Home Ministry has now announced demonstrations will no longer be permitted at Jantar Mantar. Three other sites have been listed as alternatives should permission be granted.The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the weekend protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.The BBC also captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists."Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.Rahul Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

sources.headline: Indian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme court
sources.text: Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.Security personnel stand guard at barricades in Delhi to prevent thousands of protesters reaching the supreme court. Photograph: Manish Swarup/APKumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.Security personnel detain demonstrators during a protest demanding Kumar’s resignation on Sunday. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesIn a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionThe SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.Thousands of people joined the march to the supreme court on Monday after a weekend of unrest. Photograph: Manish Swarup/APMahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the ​Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

sources.headline: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate
sources.text:
Security personnel in riot gear arrive to escort workers of India's opposition Congress party as they gather for a march toward the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, on Monday.
Manish Swarup/AP
hide caption
Manish Swarup/AP
NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.
Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists. Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.
Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution. "We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi. Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi. Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests. Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists." Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.
The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

Biman Mukherji
Published: 8:40pm, 12 Oct 2026

Indian opposition leaders and student activists marched on the Supreme Court on Monday to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over alleged voter roll manipulation, as authorities erected heavy barricades and shut six metro stations across New Delhi.

The rally went ahead after the Chief Justice of India turned down a meeting request from an opposition delegation, urging them instead to file a formal petition.

Mainstream opposition parties have sought to harness a groundswell of public anger generated by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has spearheaded weeks of protests against alleged electoral roll manipulation.

Tensions boiled over during the weekend when Delhi police detained dozens of student activists and blocked planned rallies, handing the opposition fresh political momentum for Monday’s march.

Among those held was CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was picked up by police on Saturday ahead of a demonstration that authorities said lacked official clearance due to law-and-order concerns. Dipke was released the following day alongside other activists.

Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke (centre) stands outside a court following his release in New Delhi, India, on Sunday. Photo: AP

The CJP was founded in May after India’s chief justice Chief Justice Surya Kant referred to people with fake or bogus degrees as “cockroaches”, remarks widely interpreted as a swipe at young Indians facing problems with education and employment.

Embracing the slight, Dipke launched the group as a satirical online platform that quickly morphed into a formidable street-level movement.

Although Dipke has repeatedly said the CJP is not a registered political party – describing it as a Gen Z-led pressure movement aimed at strengthening democracy – its growing momentum has led observers to speculate it could eventually enter electoral politics.

Opposition parties and student supporters have taken to the streets almost daily this month, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a recent electoral roll update known as the Special Intensive Revision. Critics and opposition leaders say the process led to the deletion of around 130 million names from draft rolls, alleging that millions of genuine voters were wrongly removed to benefit the ruling party.

The Election Commission has strongly denied the allegations, defending the removals as a routine clean-up of deceased, relocated and duplicate registrations.

In response to the weekend crackdown, the Supreme Court ruled on Sunday that peaceful, unarmed protesters in Delhi could not be detained except in accordance with legal procedures. The court also directed authorities to ensure metro and railway services operated normally – a directive swiftly tested on Monday when police closed six stations citing security concerns ahead of the march.

Police officers stand guard at a security checkpoint near Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, on Sunday. Photo: AFP

Local media reports said Rahul Gandhi, leader of the multiparty INDIA opposition alliance, had filed a petition in the Supreme Court against Kumar over alleged “vote theft”.

Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, an independent political commentator, said clamping down on the protests could prove counterproductive for the Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) federal coalition government.

“It seems the government has not been able to come up with any counterstrategy,” Mukhopadhyay said. “They are creating a certain public mood. There is a strong possibility that the CJP could take to the electoral path.”

Parallel demonstrations have broken out in major cities like Mumbai, Bengaluru and Kolkata, alongside reports of police detentions across Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and West Bengal.

“The movement is escalating and becoming far more widespread than initially thought,” said Kingshuk Nag, an author and political commentator. “It is led by students and their line of thinking is unconventional. Now, opposition parties have jumped into the fray.”

Nag added that while the BJP was adept at countering the main opposition Congress party, it would need a new playbook to handle student leaders. He drew comparisons to Arvind Kejriwal, founder of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), who launched his political career following a major 2011 anti-corruption movement. Nag said the CJP could potentially become a comparable – or even larger – political force.

Student activists take a selfie with a poster of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar during a protest in Kolkata, India, on Sunday. Photo: TNS

However, other analysts urge caution regarding the movement’s long-term impact.

Praveen Rai, a political analyst at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, pointed out that Congress previously ran a campaign centred on allegations of vote theft during state elections in West Bengal without gaining traction.

“The ongoing street protest by Congress is a manifestation of deep political frustration arising out of several electoral defeats,” Rai said, adding that the demand for the election chief’s resignation was “politically immature” and lacked credible evidence.

Nonetheless, Rai said the youth movement had galvanised the opposition to demand administrative accountability. “CJP can play an important role as a stakeholder. Elected governments tend to lose momentum and start taking things for granted if there are no active opposition parties or pressure groups.”

While India’s history has seen youth-led protests capable of toppling governments – such as the 1990 student movement over caste reservations that destabilised the VP Singh administration – Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government does not appear to be in immediate danger. The next general election is not due until 2029.

However, elections in key states including Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Punjab will offer an early test of whether this youth-driven momentum can pose a genuine threat to the BJP’s dominance.

Biman Mukherji

sources.headline: Delhi a fortress as 'cockroach' protesters show no sign of backing down
sources.text: New Delhi's Supreme Court is expected to hold a hearing on alleged vote rigging today, as protesters show no sign of backing down in the Indian capital.Six major metro stations in the Indian capital were closed yesterday and thousands of security personnel deployed to try to deter protesters attending the third straight day of protests, but protesters defied police barricades to join in the march.Rahul Gandhi, the country's main opposition Congress Party, waved a copy of the constitution as he led Monday evening's procession to the city's highest court.Protesters breach police barricades in New Delhi. (AP: Prabhat Mehrotra)Opposition parties and supporters of the "cockroach" youth movement are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the removal of millions of names from voter lists.The change has seen more than 130 million names struck from voter lists, including 28 million who had died, 63 million who had relocated, and 30 million who could not be traced.But critics claim the move benefits India Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).The Election Commission of India has denied wrongdoing, saying wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.Thousands of security personnel have been deployed across New Delhi. (AP: Manish Swarup)The petition lodged with the court on Monday night local time alleges irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.It seeks an audit of voter deletions, safeguards against deletions without notice, a hearing, and an interim suspension of the revision nationwide.The petition is expected to be heard by the Supreme Court on Tuesday.Police shut down protest siteThe protests have become a major political challenge for Mr Modi, drawing together opposition parties, student groups and activists led by the Cockroach Party movement.Opposition figures have accused authorities of trying to suppress dissent through mass detentions, but the BJP said the protests were an attempt by the main opposition party Congress to seize power.The protest is in response to a controversial revision of voter lists. (Reuters: Priyanshu Singh)"By discrediting constitutional institutions, spreading chaos and riots on the streets, and attacking people in the name of politics, all it seeks is a return to power," Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said.Barricades block every arterial road leading to Jantar Mantar, a a decades-long hub for protests.But Delhi Police have now banned the location as a protest site, identifying three new venues instead.Leader of the Samajwadi Party, Akhilesh Yadav, vows to continue the protest, saying banning the site was "the biggest defeat for the BJP government"."To avoid public outrage, it wants to keep the people away from the places where the rulers sit," he wrote on X.Monday's protest came after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crack down on New Delhi.Most of those detained, including three top leaders of the "cockroach" movement, have since been released.Parliamentarian John Brittas of the Communist Party of India alleged he was "manhandled, dragged, assaulted" by police during Sunday's demonstrations."This is not merely an assault on an MP. It is an assault on democratic freedoms and the rule of law," he said.A protester who was detained, Abhita Ruheja, said the authorities had turned Delhi into a fortress."Is this how a democracy works?" she asked."They have been scrapping rights after rights and this is turning into a dictatorship."AP/AFP

sources.headline: India's "Cockroach Party" leaders released from detention
sources.text:
Updated on: October 11, 2026 / 7:01 AM EDT
/ AP
Add CBS News on Google
Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party, an Indian youth movement, were released Sunday, a day after they were detained ahead of protests against a contentious revision of voter lists. The movement is demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.The three leaders — Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were freed on condition that they commit "no breach of peace for one year," Ratna Singh, the movement's legal director, said in a social media post. It was unclear what the condition meant or whether it would restrict their participation in protests.Police had boarded the leaders' flight from Mumbai after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday and took them into custody as they prepared to lead a demonstration in New Delhi.Authorities have launched a sweeping security crackdown in the capital, detaining more than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition lawmakers. Train services to the capital were canceled, metro stations closed and mobile internet suspended in parts of the city.Most of those detained were released late Saturday, police said.After his release, Dipke called Prime Minister Narendra Modi "an embarrassment to India.""Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he wrote on X.
